title: Quand vous serez bien vieille
greek: Quand vous serez bien vieille, au soir, à la chandelle
short: Ronsard's sonnet from the Sonnets pour Hélène (1578), II.24, here in Curtis Hidden Page's version of 1903 under Page's title 'Life's Roses'.
body: The poem first appeared in the 1578 collected edition of Ronsard's works, in the second book of the Sonnets pour Hélène; in the 1584 edition it was slightly revised and renumbered II.43. Hélène de Surgères was a maid of honour to Catherine de' Medici, and the sequence was reportedly encouraged by the queen; the ageing poet courts a young, learned and reserved woman. The French opens 'Quand vous serez bien vieille, au soir, à la chandelle'. Page (1870-1946), an American scholar and translator, published his Songs and Sonnets of Pierre de Ronsard in 1903; titles such as 'Life's Roses' are his.

title: by candlelight
short: Ronsard: 'au soir, à la chandelle, / Assise auprès du feu', in the evening, by candlelight, seated near the fire.
body: The opening is a precise domestic scene, projected into the future: the beautiful woman, now old, sits by the fire at night. Page distributes the details differently ('by the hearth's glare, / At candle-time'), and 'glare' is a rhyme-word that makes the light harsher than Ronsard's. The future tense ('serez') structures the whole poem as a prophecy addressed to the beloved.

title: spinning and winding thread
short: Ronsard's 'dévidant et filant', winding and spinning: the work of old women by the fire.
body: Spinning by the hearth is the conventional occupation of women in old age, and it fixes Hélène in a humble domestic future far from the court. Some readers also hear an allusion to the Fates, who spin and measure the thread of life, which would suit the poem's theme of mortality; the allusion is suggestive rather than certain. Page's 'winding thread' is close to 'dévidant' (reeling off yarn).

title: astonished
short: Translates 'en vous émerveillant', marvelling; Page's metre needs a stressed final syllable, 'astonishèd'.
body: Ronsard's Hélène will recite the poems 'en vous émerveillant', wondering at them, and at the fact that she was their subject. In Page's line the rhyme with 'thread' and 'said' requires the old pronunciation with the -ed sounded. The surprise is double-edged: she marvels at the poems, but also at having once been beautiful. Page's 'say, astonished' thus makes the old Hélène an amazed reader of her own legend.

anchor: Ronsard made these for me, when I was fair
title: Ronsard made these for me
greek: Ronsard me célébrait du temps que j'étais belle
short: Ronsard: 'Ronsard me célébrait du temps que j'étais belle', Ronsard celebrated me when I was beautiful. The poet names himself.
body: The poet puts his own name in the mouth of the old woman, and the line is the poem's hinge: her beauty is past, but his poetry, and so his name, survives. This is the classical boast of the poet who confers immortality, as in Horace's 'non omnis moriar' (Odes 3.30), which Ronsard imitated elsewhere (see his 'Permanet Gloria' in this archive). Page's 'made these for me' turns 'célébrait' (celebrated, sang the praises of) into making, which suits Ronsard's sense of poetry as craft.

title: the half-sleeping servant
short: Ronsard: no servant of yours, half-asleep over her work, will fail to wake at the sound ('au bruit') of Ronsard's name.
body: The second quatrain imagines the poet's fame reaching even the household servant: 'Lors vous n'aurez servante oyant telle nouvelle, / Déjà sous le labeur à demi sommeillant, / Qui au bruit de Ronsard ne s'aille réveillant'. The phrase 'au bruit de Ronsard' means at the sound, and also the renown, of Ronsard. Page omits the poet's name here and makes the servant wake at 'what you have said'; his 'toil and care / Almost out-worn' renders 'sous le labeur à demi sommeillant'.

anchor: bless your name with deathless praise
title: bless your name
greek: Bénissant votre nom de louange immortelle
short: Ronsard: 'Bénissant votre nom de louange immortelle'. The immortal praise is Hélène's, but only because Ronsard gave it.
body: The participle 'bénissant' grammatically belongs to the servant, who blesses Hélène's name. The poem's logic, however, is that Hélène's immortality depends wholly on the poet: her name lives because his verse praised it. Critics have often noted the barbed compliment, and the mixture of flattery and threat in the sonnet as a whole. Page's 'fore'er' is a rhyme-driven addition. The tone has been read both as tender and as vindictive.

anchor: My bones shall lie in earth
title: My bones shall lie in earth
short: Ronsard: 'Je serai sous la terre et fantôme sans os', I shall be under the earth, a boneless ghost. Page reverses the image.
body: Ronsard's phrase 'fantôme sans os' separates the body in the grave from the bodiless shade in the underworld: the ghost has no bones. Page's 'My bones shall lie in earth, and my poor ghost / Take its long rest' divides them in a different way, keeping the bones and losing Ronsard's striking paradox. The first tercet shifts from Hélène's future to the poet's, in the plain future tense of the opening.

title: Love's dark myrtles
greek: Par les ombres myrteux; Lat. myrtea silva
short: Ronsard: 'Par les ombres myrteux je prendrai mon repos'. The myrtle shades recall Virgil's Fields of Mourning for those who died of love.
body: In Aeneid 6.440-44 Aeneas sees the 'lugentes campi', the Mourning Fields of the underworld, where those whom cruel love consumed wander hidden in a myrtle wood ('myrtea circum / silva tegit'); Dido is among them. The myrtle was sacred to Venus. Ronsard's lover thus expects to lie among love's martyrs. Page's 'Love's dark myrtles' makes the association explicit by adding 'Love's'.

title: crouching by the fire
short: Ronsard: 'Vous serez au foyer une vieille accroupie', you will be an old woman crouched at the hearth.
body: The second tercet returns to Hélène's future with brutal realism: 'accroupie' (squatting, huddled) is an unflattering word, and 'vieille' used as a noun (an old woman) is blunter still. The contrast between the poet's dignified rest among the myrtles and the woman's huddled old age is the poem's threat. Page's 'old, shrunken, grey' adds adjectives of his own. The tercet balances 'Je serai' (I shall be) against 'Vous serez' (you will be).

title: Yeats's 'When You Are Old'
short: W. B. Yeats's 'When You Are Old' (1892) is a free adaptation of this sonnet, written for Maud Gonne.
body: Yeats's poem opens 'When you are old and grey and full of sleep, / And nodding by the fire, take down this book', clearly modelled on Ronsard's scene of the old woman by the fire reading the poet's verses. Yeats drops Ronsard's threat and his carpe diem ending and instead imagines regret for 'the pilgrim soul' that one man loved. Page, translating a decade later, includes 'grey' in his version, perhaps with Yeats's line in his ear, though that cannot be proved.

title: proud disdain
short: Ronsard: 'Regrettant mon amour et votre fier dédain', regretting my love and your proud disdain.
body: The haughty disdain of the beloved is the Petrarchan donna's defining trait, and Ronsard turns it against her: in old age she will regret both his lost love and her own pride. 'Rue' in Page means to regret bitterly (OED, rue, v.1). Page's ellipsis after 'lost' marks the turn from prophecy to exhortation. The word 'fier' means proud or haughty, not 'fierce'.

title: Wait not to-morrow
greek: n'attendez à demain; Lat. carpe diem
short: Ronsard: 'Vivez, si m'en croyez, n'attendez à demain', live, if you believe me, do not wait for tomorrow: Horace's carpe diem.
body: The last two lines of the sonnet give the poem's moral, drawn from Horace, Odes 1.11.8: 'carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero' ('pluck the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow'). Ronsard's 'si m'en croyez' echoes Horace's 'credula'. Page translates it as 'hear me, love!' and repeats 'live' at the start and end of the line, framing the injunction; the dashes are his.

title: the roses of life
greek: Cueillez dès aujourd'hui les roses de la vie; Lat. collige, virgo, rosas
short: Ronsard: 'Cueillez dès aujourd'hui les roses de la vie', gather from today the roses of life: the classical rose topos.
body: The image of gathering roses before they fade comes from the Latin poem 'De rosis nascentibus' attributed to Ausonius, which ends 'collige, virgo, rosas' ('gather roses, girl'), and is anticipated in the Wisdom of Solomon, where the ungodly say 'Let us crown ourselves with rosebuds, before they be withered' (2:8). Ronsard used the topos repeatedly (compare 'Mignonne, allons voir si la rose', in the archive as 'Sweet-heart, come see if the rose'); it passes into English in Spenser and Herrick. Page's 'oh! to-day, to-day' adds an emotional repetition.

title: metre and rhyme
short: Ronsard writes in alexandrines rhymed ABBA ABBA CCD EED; Page uses English pentameter rhymed ABBA ABBA CDE CDE.
body: The French twelve-syllable line gives Ronsard's sonnet a slow, measured gravity. Page translates into iambic pentameter, which forces compression and some padding (fore'er, oh!). His sestet rhyme (ghost, thrive, grey; lost, live, to-day) differs from Ronsard's French pattern, with 'thrive/live' only an eye-rhyme. The archive prints the sonnet in quatrains and tercets, and Page closes on a doubled 'to-day', where Ronsard ends on 'les roses de la vie'.
